title: Inclusive For Whom, and at What Cost?
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (theartofaskingquestions.com), November 1, 2026
summary: Chiarelli opens a planned series arguing that diversity and inclusion are harder than popular slogans suggest, not that they are misguided. Near-universal statements such as 'Everyone should feel included' stop being unobjectionable the moment they must become a meeting format, hiring process or performance metric, because different people need different things and some needs collide. He treats inclusion as a design problem with constraints, trade-offs and costs, and offers examples such as standardized processes that reduce bias but block individual accommodation, or disclosure that enables support but invites stigma. Drawing on meta-analyses by Traylor and Wallrich, he notes the average link between diversity and team performance is positive but very small, and he uses Shore's belonging-plus-uniqueness framing to separate inclusion from assimilation. Neurodiversity serves as the case study, where the popular 'superpower' language runs ahead of thin evidence. His conclusion is that no workplace is universally inclusive, and the useful question is inclusive for whom, under what conditions and at what cost, with the cost named and its bearer identified.
points: Inclusion is a design problem, not common sense: attitude is a starting condition, and real decisions about meetings, assignments, evaluation and space always involve trade-offs.
Trade-offs left unnamed still get made, usually invisibly and in favor of whoever fits the default.

The performance case for diversity is weak at the average level: large syntheses find a positive but very small link, so the moral and legal arguments carry more weight than promised performance gains.
Shore's framework defines inclusion as belongingness plus uniqueness; belonging without uniqueness is assimilation, and uniqueness without belonging is marginal tolerance.
Replace 'Is this workplace inclusive?' with 'Inclusive for whom, under what conditions and at what cost, and who carries it?'
quotes: A sentence everyone endorses cannot effectively guide everyday workplace practice, and it’s even less useful when things go badly wrong.
Attitude matters, of course, but we should consider it a starting condition, not a method.
Design problems have constraints, trade-offs and costs. They improve through iteration and evidence, not through goodwill.
An organisation that pretends there are no trade-offs will still make them. It will just make them invisibly, and usually in favour of whoever happens to fit the default.
In short, diversity can increase the range of perspectives available to a team. But it can also increase the work required to integrate them.
Belonging without uniqueness is assimilation. Uniqueness without belonging often results in being tolerated at the margins. Only the two together amount to inclusion.
Celebrating cognitive differences is easy enough. Designing workplaces intentionally and meaningfully around cognitive differences is much harder
A realist asks for the cost to be named, and then asks who is carrying it.
An organisation that can say “Here is what we are trading off, and why” is closer to inclusion than one that can only say “Everyone is welcome”.
